name: Aburatorigami oil-blotting paper

lead: Aburatorigami (Japanese for "oil removal paper") is a thin, absorbent paper traditionally made from abaca fibre. Pressed onto the skin, it soaks up surface sebum so the forehead, nose and cheeks look less shiny.

The appearance payoff is a matte, even-looking complexion that photographs and wears better through the day, without removing or smudging makeup. The effect is short-lived, since the skin keeps producing oil.

paras: People press a sheet gently against oily areas, usually the T-zone, and lift it away, without rubbing. They use it midday, before photos or between makeup touch-ups. Sheets are sold in small booklets by Japanese and international cosmetic brands.

Blotting has little risk when done gently; rubbing can irritate skin. It removes oil without changing how much the skin produces. Accounts of its effect on acne are mixed and rest on limited sources, and one report cited in a Grokipedia article describes reduced sunscreen protection after blotting, so sunscreen is generally reapplied afterward per product guidance.

angle.text: Pressing a sheet onto the T-zone removes visible surface oil and shine on the spot, so skin looks matte and makeup looks fresher. The effect is temporary because oil production continues.

lead: Aburatorigami (あぶらとり紙, "oil removal paper") is a traditional Japanese facial blotting paper used to absorb excess oil and reduce shine.[1] It is a close relative of the oil-blotting sheets sold by cosmetic brands worldwide, which are used to absorb sebum from the face.[2]

People use it to keep a matte, even-looking complexion through the day: pressing a sheet onto the forehead, nose and chin removes surface oil that would otherwise make skin look shiny in person or in photographs.[1][3] Because it lifts oil from the surface only, the effect lasts roughly half an hour to an hour in one summary, after which sebum returns.[3]
Its origins are traced to gold-leaf production in Kanazawa and Kyoto, and it later became associated with geisha and kabuki performers.[1]

paras: Traditional aburatorigami is made from the finest grade of abaca leaf rather than wood pulp, with no oil-based chemicals, according to Wikipedia's account.[1] Cosmetic versions can also use other fibres such as washi, rice paper, bamboo or jute.[3] Modern facial blotting sheets worldwide are often dyed and may be dusted with salicylic acid and minerals.[2]

The paper was first known as hakuuchi-gami, used by Kanazawa gold artisans to protect gold during goldbeating, and demand rose in the Heian period (794-1192) as it was taken to Kyoto to wrap gold leaf.[1] People later noticed that the paper also absorbed oil from skin, and its popularity grew in the Edo period (1603-1867).[1]

Kabuki actors and geisha used it to keep traditional white makeup (oshiroi) fresh during long performances, including in non-air-conditioned theatres such as the Minamiza in Kyoto.[1] Gold artisans are said to have given sheets to geisha as small gifts.[1] Today it is used for everyday skincare and makeup by women and men.[1]

Users press a thin sheet onto oily areas, mainly the T-zone, to take up surface sebum without disturbing makeup.[3] Experts quoted in one summary advise pressing rather than rubbing and limiting use to two or three times a day.[3]

Wikipedia notes claims that the paper balances water and oil in skin and helps prevent skin problems, supported only by older non-scientific sources.[1] A Grokipedia summary states that blotting removes oil but does not reduce sebum production, reports a 2021 study in which blotting reduced sunscreen SPF by about a third, and gives inconsistent accounts of a 2022 acne study.[3] Whether blotting helps or worsens acne is described as disputed on Wikipedia's blotting-paper page.[2]
No studies found. A Grokipedia summary mentions a 2021 study on sunscreen reduction after blotting and a 2022 acne study, but the underlying papers were not verified.[3]

timeline.event: Heian period: demand for the gold-leaf by-product paper rises as it is carried to Kyoto.[1]
Edo period: the paper grows popular for refreshing the complexion.[1]
